questions.question: Define a development indicator and explain why several indicators should be used.
questions.expected_answer: An indicator is a measurable piece of information linked to an aspect of development, such as income, life expectancy, literacy or access to water. Indicators allow comparison between places, tracking change over time, targeting help and evaluating policy. Types include economic, social, demographic, environmental and political. Each measures only part of development and has limitations, so geographers use a set of indicators or a composite index such as the HDI.

questions.question: Explain GDP per capita, show how it is calculated and give two limitations.
questions.expected_answer: GDP is the total value of final goods and services produced in a country in a year; GDP per capita is GDP divided by population, e.g. 380 billion dollars divided by 62 million people gives about 6 100 dollars. PPP adjusts for local prices (South Africa about 15 000 dollars PPP). Limitations: it is an average that hides inequality (South Africa's Gini about 0,63); it omits unpaid and informal work; it counts harmful activity and ignores environmental damage.

questions.question: Explain life expectancy and infant mortality as indicators of development, including how infant mortality is calculated.
questions.expected_answer: Life expectancy is the average number of years a newborn can expect to live, reflecting nutrition, health care, water and safety (about 84 in Japan; low to mid sixties in South Africa after recovering from HIV). Infant mortality is infant deaths before age one per 1 000 live births, e.g. 1 200 deaths among 48 000 births gives 25 per 1 000. A lower rate indicates higher development because it depends on maternal health, skilled birth care, clean water, vaccines and mothers' education.
